title: The truths expounded
hookLine: Sariputta sets out the four truths in detail

cards: The Deer Park at Isipatana, near Benares: in the tradition, the place where the Buddha first taught the four noble truths to five companions. In the hundred and forty-first discourse, he's there again.
He reminds the monks that the wheel of the teaching was first set rolling right here, by announcing four truths. Then he does something a good teacher does. He points to two students.
Go to Sariputta and Moggallana, he says. Learn from them. And he goes into his dwelling.

teach.b: Before he leaves, the Buddha gives a picture of his two chief students. Sariputta is like a mother who gives birth; Moggallana, like a nurse who raises the child. Sariputta trains people to the first real breakthrough.
Moggallana trains them to the highest goal. So Sariputta addresses the monks and does what the title says: he expounds. He takes each truth and opens it.
First, suffering. Birth is suffering, and he defines birth, the coming into being of beings. Aging is suffering: gray hair, wrinkled skin, failing faculties.
Death, sorrow, grief, despair, each named and described. Not getting what you want is suffering. And in short, the five heaps that are clung to are suffering.
Second, the origin: craving that leads to renewed being, craving for pleasure, for becoming, for non-becoming. Third, the cessation: the complete fading and ending of that craving, letting it go.

Fourth, the path, and he defines each of the eight factors one by one, from right view, knowing these four truths, to right concentration. Nothing dramatic happens. No one is suddenly freed in the story.
It's a careful lecture, almost a textbook, and that's the point.
The four truths can be announced in a minute, as the Buddha did at the start. But they're meant to be unfolded, slowly, word by word, by students who've learned them well enough to teach.
Expounded means laid out, line by line, so others can walk through it.

how: The four noble truths are taught in Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana schools alike, and the detailed analysis in MN 141 has a close parallel in the Digha Nikaya's great discourse on the foundations of mindfulness (DN 22).

games.q: the truths expounded: tap the pairs.
p: like a mother who gives birth
like a nurse who raises the child
craving that leads to renewed being
where the wheel was first set rolling

s: in MN 141 the Buddha expounds the truths himself, at length
he points the monks to Sariputta and Moggallana and goes inside; Sariputta expounds them.
Sariputta defines each factor of the eightfold path
from right view, knowing the four truths, through right concentration.
the discourse says the five heaps that are clung to are suffering, in short
after naming birth, aging, death and more, Sariputta sums them up that way.

games.q: the Buddha compares his two chief students to a mother and a nurse. which is Sariputta?
o: the nurse who raises the child.
games.why: Sariputta is the mother, training people to the first breakthrough; Moggallana the nurse, training them to the highest goal.

practice: In your own words, slowly, say one line with each out-breath: there is suffering; it has a cause, craving; it can end; there is a path.
Then go around again, and let each line touch something real from your week: a small ache, a want, a moment of ease, a step you took.

wordCard.voice: Sacca. Truth: at the Deer Park, Sariputta lays out the four noble truths, the ariya saccas, in detail, defining each one word by word. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sacca: truth. Sanskrit satya. the four ariya saccas are the noble truths.

carryVoice: Your line: expounded. Four short truths, opened one word at a time. That's day five hundred seven.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 141, Saccavibhanga Sutta (the exposition of the truths)
